To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the arsenic binding site in the arsenic repressor, AfarsR, is located at the ends the C-terminal helices and that this site is different from the site in R773 ArsR.
a new As(III) coordination site, S3, has been discovered in the ArsR family of metallo-regulators and that this site is located at the ends of C-terminal helices of the protein.
the ArsRs from Acidithiobaccillus ferrooxidants and Escherichiocoli evolved different As(III) - binding sites that are located at different spatial positions in their three-dimensional structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the ArsRs and other members of the ArsR family of metallotranscriptional regulators have evolved to recognize and respond to a diverse array of metals and metalloids.
the convergent evolution of As(III)-binding sites in the ArsR family of metallotranscription factors.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate bacterial arsenic resistance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the arsenic binding sites in the ArsR proteins from Acidithiobactillus ferrooxidants and plasmid R774 arose independently through convergent evolution.
the arsenic binding sites of the ArsRs evolved independently and that the arsenic repressor genes are convergently evolving.
As(III)-sensitive ArsRs have arisen independently in at least two lineages, one in the gamma-proteobacteria and another in the acidophilic bacteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ArsR/SMTB family of metal sensors have evolved a new As(III) sensing mechanism, which is not shared with other metalloregulatory families.

As(III)-dependent regulation by ArsR/Smtb family members is not limited to a single As(III)-binding site and that convergent evolution of new As(III)-specific binding sites has occurred at least twice in the ArsR family.

the ArsR/SMTB family of metal sensing transcriptional repressors has undergone convergent evolution in two different organisms to create two different As(III) responsive transcriptional repressor systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ArsR family of metalloregulated transcriptional repressors has undergone convergent evolution to produce arsenic binding sites in two different locations in its three-dimensional structure.
the ArsR/SMTB family of metal sensing proteins has evolved at least three distinct As(III)-binding sites that can be found in different organisms.
the ArsR/SMTB family of metal sensors has evolved to bind As(III) in a number of different ways, and the As(III), Zn(II), Cd(II), and Cu(I) binding sites are not homologous.
